phonemes.desc: Voiceless glottal [h] plus long open-mid front [ɛː] with acute pitch — the stressed, lengthened syllable.
Voiced bilabial [b] plus long open-mid front [ɛː]; the two long syllables frame the name.

pronunciation.approximation: 'HEH-beh' — both syllables long and even, the first pitched higher. English 'HEE-bee' is the later, Latinized sound.

kin.label: Greek noun
kin.form: ἥβη (hēbē), 'youth, the bloom of early strength' — the word she personifies (LSJ, s.v. ἥβη)

kin.label: Greek verb
kin.form: ἡβάω (hēbáō), 'to be in one's prime' — the same root, in verbal form

kin.label: Roman equivalent
kin.form: Juventas, 'Youth' — her interpretatio; vowed a temple in 218 BCE (Livy 36.36)

pronunciation.note: Greek Ἥβη carries both features the mechanical rule requires: acute stress on ἥ and the long vowel η — so the name is Tier-1. The registrable restoration 'Hebe' is plain ASCII and preserves neither; the tier speaks for the original Greek, never for the alphabet.

domains.title: Hebe
domains.subtitle: Youth
domains.lead: Hebe is youth in its most literal Greek sense — ἥβη, the bloom of early strength — made goddess: cupbearer of Olympus, wife of the deified Herakles, and the only figure in the pantheon whose name is her domain. Hers is a small mythology with a large office: keeping the immortals fed, and keeping the idea of youth itself enthroned.

cards.name: Nectar and Ambrosia
cards.desc: As cupbearer she poured the gods' immortal food — the office shown on countless vases with oinochoe and phiale.

cards.name: Youth Itself
cards.desc: Her name means 'Youth' (ἥβη): the bloom of early strength that peaks, passes, and never returns.

cards.name: The Bride of Herakles
cards.desc: After his labors the hero ascended to Olympus and made her his wife — the one apotheosis Greece awarded (Odyssey 11.601–604).

cards.name: Ganymede's Predecessor
cards.desc: She held the cupbearer office before Zeus gave it to the Trojan prince Ganymede (Iliad 20.231–235).

symbols.name: Oinochoe and phiale
symbols.meaning: Pitcher and shallow cup — the instruments of the cupbearer, her fixed attribute on Attic vases

symbols.name: Nectar and ambrosia
symbols.meaning: The food and drink of immortality, whose pouring was her eternal office

symbols.name: The fillet
symbols.meaning: The youth's headband — the mark of ἥβη itself, worn by the goddess who is youth

symbols.name: The wedding wreath
symbols.meaning: The stephanos of her marriage to Herakles, closing the greatest heroic career with immortality

symbols.name: The spring at Phlius
symbols.meaning: The sanctuary city that alone gave her a civic cult (Pausanias 2.13.3) — the permanent address of the most fleeting gift

mythology.lead: The stories of Hebe are short, and all Olympian housekeeping: she pours for the gods, loses her office, marries the burned hero, and keeps a single small temple. Yet the homeliness is the point — youth, in this mythology, is not a protagonist but a substance the gods drink.

myths.title: Nectar for the Gods
myths.text: On Olympus the youngest of the goddesses had the oldest of duties. Hebe — her very name means 'Youth' — poured nectar and ambrosia for the gods at their golden tables and kept their cups filled through quarrels, weddings, and feasts. Homer gives her the homelier tasks too: after Ares staggers back from the field with a spear-wound the size of a fist, it is Hebe who bathes him and dresses him again in fine clothing (Iliad 5.904–906). On Attic vases she appears again and again in this role, oinochoe in one hand, phiale in the other, forever refilling the cup that keeps the immortals immortal. The myth encodes a simple economy: on Olympus, even the food of eternity must be served — and it is served by youth itself, because only the young have the inexhaustible hands.

myths.title: Why Ganymede Has the Cup
myths.text: Late sources tell why Hebe lost her office, and they are honest enough to admit the tale is not Homer's. While serving at a ceremony on Olympus — the scholiasts and Eustathius place the episode at Olympia during the founding rites — Hebe fell. Some say she stumbled, some that the fall stripped her bare, and the humiliation cost her the cupbearer service; Zeus gave the office to the beautiful Trojan prince Ganymede, 'for his beauty's sake, to be among the immortals and pour wine' (Iliad 20.231–235). The same late commentators preserve a stranger detail: from her magic girdle the Eleans drew rites against old age. The story is a parable of how fragile even a divine job can be — youth serves at the table only until it trips, and the cup passes to a newer face.

myths.title: Herakles Ascends
myths.text: When Herakles had burned away his mortal part on the pyre at Oita, the divine portion of him was carried up to Olympus, and there he received the reward no other hero won: Hebe. 'He made Hebe, with her beautiful ankles, daughter of great Zeus and of Hera of the golden sandals, his wife' (Odyssey 11.601–604); Hesiod sets the wedding among the unions that settled the divine order (Theogony 950–955). By her the hero — now wholly a god — fathered the twin guardians Alexiares and Aniketos, 'Averter of Evil' and 'Unconquered' (Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.7.7). The marriage closes the greatest career of Greek myth with its most radical promise: that youth itself can be the prize of endurance, and that the man who burned could still be given forever.

myths.title: The One Temple of Youth
myths.text: For a goddess so close to the throne of Zeus, Hebe received remarkably little civic worship — one city excepted. At Phlius in the northeastern Peloponnese stood her sanctuary, with an ancient cult image, and the Phliasians were known throughout Greece for honoring the daughter of Zeus and Hera where other cities neglected her (Pausanias 2.13.3). The choice of Phlius is telling: a small, conservative city guarding one archaic cult exactly as it had received it — no Panhellenic games, no oracle, no treasure, just a single temple where youth, the most fleeting of the gods' gifts, was given a permanent address. Pausanias adds the local pride: the Phliasians said their Hebe was honored there from the earliest times, and they tended her image with the stubborn care of a family heirloom. The cult quietly argues the theology of her name: what passes fastest deserves the shrine most.

lore.syncretism: Rome knew her as Juventas, 'Youth', and gave her what Greece had almost withheld: a temple in the Forum Boarium, vowed by C. Licinius Lucullus during the darkest year of the Hannibalic War (218 BCE) and dedicated by M. Livius Salinator in 191 (Livy 36.36). There she stood at the gate through which new citizens passed into public life, patroness of the moment a Roman youth assumed the toga virilis. The identification is exact — Juventas simply translates Ἥβη — and it quietly upgrades the Greek picture: where Hebe was a servant of the Olympian table, Juventas was installed at the threshold of the Roman state, making youth itself a civic and military virtue worth a temple inside the city walls.
lore.culturalLegacy: Juventas vanished with the temples, but Hebe kept her name in three worlds. In art she became a favorite subject of eighteenth- and nineteenth-century painters — Rubens, Canova and a hundred lesser hands staged the wedding with Herakles and the cupbearer at the Olympian table. In astronomy, 6 Hebe is a main-belt asteroid discovered in 1847, among the earliest asteroids ever found. In botany, Hebe is a genus of flowering shrubs native to New Zealand, christened for the goddess by naturalists who carried the classical world to the South Pacific. Each reuse tells the same story: the Greeks packed the whole meaning of youth into two syllables, and everyone since has been borrowing them.
lore.extendedMeditation: Hebe is the goddess of what no one keeps. Youth, in the Greek imagination, is not a stage you remember; it is a substance the gods drink. That is why the mythology gives the youngest goddess the most repetitive job on Olympus — pouring, refilling, pouring again — and why the only city that built her a temple was a small one, Phlius (Pausanias 2.13.3). Some gifts are so universal they escape notice; some are so brief they deserve a permanent address. Her marriage to Herakles completes the thought. The hero who burned off his mortality did not receive wisdom, or prophecy, or wealth — he received youth, forever, in the person of its goddess. To be made a god, in this telling, is precisely to stop losing ἥβη. It is the Greek answer to every human grief: not that youth returns, but that somewhere it never left the table.
lore.originalScriptNote: The Greek is Ἥβη. The acute on ἥ marks the stress, and the eta η is a long vowel — ἥβη is long in both syllables. PUNICODEX writes the plain-ASCII 'Hebe', the registrable form, while the tier speaks for the original Greek, which carries both features.
